title: Polycarp (c. 155)
hook: the old bishop refuses to curse Christ: eighty-six years I have served him

segments.voice: Yesterday, pharmakon athanasias, Ignatius's medicine of immortality, kept with the bishop. Your line was one bread, one bishop.

Swear the oath, curse Christ, and I'll let you go. A Roman governor says it in a packed stadium in Smyrna, to a very old man. The crowd is shouting. The governor presses again and again, and threatens wild beasts, then fire. The old man is Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna. Ignatius once wrote him a letter on the road to Rome. His answer to the governor is not an argument. It's a number.
screen: `A STADIUM IN SMYRNA.` → `REVILE THE CHRIST.` → `AN OLD MAN ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: His answer, in Lightfoot's translation of the Martyrdom of Polycarp: "Fourscore and six years have I been His servant, and He hath done me no wrong. How then can I blaspheme my King who saved me?" Eighty-six years: a life added up. First, the source: a letter from the church of Smyrna to another church, telling what happened to their bishop. Second, the arrest. When soldiers find him at a farm outside the city, he comes down and talks with them. He has food and drink set out for them, as much as they want, and asks only for an hour to pray. He prays standing, remembering everyone he has ever met, small and great, for two hours, until some of the soldiers are sorry they came. Third, the stadium. As he walks in, the account says, a voice comes from heaven: be strong, Polycarp, and play the man. The governor tells him to respect his age, and to say: away with the atheists. That's what the crowd called Christians, because they wouldn't worship the gods. Polycarp looks at the crowd, waves his hand toward them, sighs, looks up to heaven, and says it: away with the atheists. He just means a different crowd. Fourth, what his church did next. They gathered his bones, more precious than jewels, they said, and planned to meet there to keep what they called the birthday of his martyrdom. The Catholic calendar still marks many saints on the day they died, which it calls their birth into heaven. Polycarp's church turned a death day into a birthday.
screen: `A LETTER FROM SMYRNA.` · `FOOD FOR THE SOLDIERS, AN HOUR TO PRAY.` · `AWAY WITH THE ATHEISTS.` · `THE BIRTHDAY OF HIS MARTYRDOM.` · then, large: `FOURSCORE AND SIX YEARS.`

segments.voice: Say your age to yourself, then let the years go by in chunks: childhood, school, the first job, the move, the loss, the person who changed things. Don't stop to judge any of it; Polycarp didn't say every year was easy, only that the One he served had done him no wrong. If you pray, give thanks one stretch at a time; if you don't, notice that you're still here, and what carried you.
Polycarp. The old bishop of Smyrna who would not curse Christ after a lifetime of serving him. Today's word.
Your line: eighty-six years. A lifetime of faithfulness, said in one number. Day seven hundred five.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Polycarp each year, and the Church's calendar often sets a saint's day on the day of death, called the birth into heaven.

chat.says: What did Polycarp mean when he said eighty-six years?
options: He'd served Christ eighty-six years and been done no wrong, so how could he curse him?
It was his age when he became bishop, so he refused to give up the office.
He was asking the governor for eighty-six more days to put his affairs in order.
chat.meaning: Told to curse Christ, Polycarp answered that he had served him eighty-six years and been done no wrong: how could he blaspheme his King?

notes: Both quotations from Martyrdom of Polycarp 9 attributed to Lightfoot (Apostolic Fathers, 1891): confirm exact wording and the translator before publication; if not exact, paraphrase.
'Eighty-six years' is the text's own number (ch. 9). Whether it counts from birth or baptism is debated; script doesn't say.

Paraphrases: ch. 7 (food and drink for the soldiers, an hour to pray, two hours, some sorry they came); ch. 9 (voice from heaven, 'away with the atheists'); ch. 12 (crowd's charges); ch. 18 (bones, birthday of his martyrdom). Confirm.
'The Church still keeps its saints' days this way' links the dies natalis custom to this text as an early example; Keeper to confirm wording, which avoids calling it the first.
Title date 'c. 155' is the index's; dating is debated (c. 155–167). No date in the voice.

Audit: the hook repeated the governor's offer twice ('one curse, and go home'); the second now says he keeps pressing and threatens beasts and fire (ch. 9-11). Garbled 'planned to gather to keep' fixed.

Editor: the governor's line was quoted in wording not verified against Lightfoot (who has 'Swear the oath'), so it is now paraphrased with quoted null; cut 'would rather not kill a grandfather' (not in the text) and the stock 'one of the lines the Church keeps'; 'meet each year' to 'gather' (ch. 18 gives no 'each year'); 'The Church still keeps its saints' days this way' softened (not every feast is a death day); howItsDone drops 'many keep patron feasts' (repeated y2 day 694's angle).
